As for your question, humans have been aware of the existence of outer space for thousands of years. The earliest recorded observations of the night sky date back to ancient civilizations in Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Greece. These cultures recognized the stars and constellations, and some even believed that the stars were gods or spirits.

The idea that space was a void of darkness illuminated only by stars and galaxies developed over time as our understanding of the universe evolved. In ancient Greece, philosophers such as Aristotle and Epicurus proposed that the universe was infinite and contained a vast expanse of empty space.

However, it wasn't until the 16th century that the concept of a vast, dark universe began to take shape. The Polish astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus proposed a heliocentric model of the universe, where the Sun was at the center and the planets orbited around it. This idea challenged the geocentric model, which placed Earth at the center of the universe.

The first person to propose that space was a void of darkness was the German astronomer Johannes Kepler in the early 17th century. Kepler observed that the stars and galaxies were not fixed in place, but were instead moving through space. He also realized that the universe was much larger than previously thought, and that the stars and galaxies were spread out over vast distances.

The modern understanding of outer space as a vast, dark universe was further developed by scientists such as Galileo Galilei, Isaac Newton, and Albert Einstein. These scientists made significant contributions to our understanding of the universe, including the discovery of black holes, dark matter, and dark energy.

As for the idea that space was blue like the morning sky, this is a misconception that has been debunked by scientists. The color of space is actually black, as it absorbs all wavelengths of light. The stars and galaxies we see in the night sky appear white or blue because they emit light of all wavelengths, but the space itself is not blue.

In summary, humans have been aware of the existence of outer space for thousands of years, and our understanding of the universe has evolved over time. While the idea that space was a void of darkness illuminated only by stars and galaxies developed over time, it was not until the 16th century that the concept of a vast, dark universe began to take shape.
